chapters.title: Sales Performance
facts: Sales revenue was ₹15,29,410 from 196 distinct sales and 139 buyers. Average spend per buyer was ₹11,003; recorded item discounts were 8.7% of sales revenue plus discounts.
Sales revenue is payment receipts. Delivered session revenue describes attended activity; the two totals are not a purchase-usage reconciliation.
chapters.subtitle: Sales were 2.3% lower than last September
recs_extra: Re-price the ladder so the bigger commitment is always cheaper per class
Sales + Finance
Newcomers 2 For 1 sells at ₹971 a class while Single Class sells at ₹1,943; 38 lines went out at the dearer per-class rate.

Moving even a quarter of the 69 class-count sales onto the best per-class tier adds credits to the delivered base at no revenue cost, and removes the single clearest pricing inconsistency on the board.
Sell the second purchase while the first is being served
Front Desk
36 of 139 buyers bought more than once and produced 25% of the cash. 74% bought once and were not offered anything further.

A renewal conversation at the moment of highest engagement is worth more than the same conversation in an email three weeks later; on this month’s mix it is the difference between a one-purchase member and a repeat one.
Put every discount code under one owner and one ceiling
Marketing + Finance
4 codes were used in September 2026, giving away ₹1,45,209 at depths between 10% and 19%. The largest single code is 42% of all discounting.
One owner and one depth cap turns discounting from a leak into a lever, and makes the month comparable to next month.
Own the interval between the first visit and the second
Front Desk + Studio Manager
Members who came back within a day of a first visit are worth ₹17,058 across a lifetime; those who took over a month are worth ₹8,367.
Booking the next class before the member leaves the building converts the only moment when they are certain they want to come back.

chapters.title: Class Performance
facts: 259 sessions delivered 1,404 attendances across 3,293 available seats. Utilisation was 42.6%; average attendance was 5.42 per session.
Utilisation is total attendances divided by total capacity. It is not the average of individual session percentages.
chapters.subtitle: Fewer sessions, a higher share of seats filled
recs_extra: Recover the 65 booked seats PowerCycle leaves empty
Studio Manager + Programming
PowerCycle is the largest single source of unoccupied booked seats this month: 65 of them, on a 86% show rate against a studio-wide 88%.

The scale of the format is what makes the number worth chasing: one class a week tighter, or a waitlist that fires the moment a seat returns, recovers roughly 16 seats a month without a single new member being asked for money.
Review every class that ran to nobody before it is scheduled again
Programming
11 classes in September 2026 were taught to an empty room, concentrated in PowerCycle (8).
Each one is a paid hour that produced nothing. A monthly rule - three empties and the slot is retired or re-timed - is the cheapest capacity the studio has.
Close or re-time the hour nobody uses
Programming + Studio Manager
16:00 fills at 71% while 20:00 fills at 11% on 2 classes.
Moving an hour of capacity from the weakest slot to the strongest is a same-month change to utilisation that needs no new members, no price change and no marketing spend.
Set a minimum viable class size and publish it
Programming
38 classes ran to one or two people out of 259. A room of two costs the same as a room of ten and reads, to the member in it, as a class nobody wants.
Merging thin classes into the adjacent slot protects the format and raises the perceived quality of both.
Give event classes a purpose and a number
Marketing + Studio Manager
3 hosted or partner sessions took 34 attendances (2%) and ₹0 of revenue on 1% of the month\’s capacity.
Decide in advance whether each event is buying reach or making money, and the next month can be judged on the one that was chosen.

chapters.title: Instructor Performance
facts: 14 instructors delivered the month’s 259 sessions. Review recorded attendance, capacity and delivered revenue by instructor, then compare like-for-like hours and formats.
Assigned slots and formats differ. Rankings alone do not establish an instructor effect.
chapters.subtitle: Read instructor results alongside their slots
recs_extra: Give Anmol Sharma the slots that already work
Studio Manager
Anmol Sharma fills 29.1% of 21 classes, the lowest on the roster, at ₹1,022 of revenue per attendee.
Re-timing rather than removing is the change: the same hands in a better hour usually closes half the gap without a single class being cut.
Pay for attendance, not for the size of the room
Studio Manager + Finance
Raunak Khemuka delivers ₹1,329 of class revenue per attendee against a roster average of ₹931. Cost per attendance, not per class, is what decides whether an hour was worth having.
A rate anchored to attendance aligns the trainer, the timetable and the P&L on the same number and ends the incentive to fill a big room badly.
Assign first classes deliberately, by conversion
Programming + Sales
Conversion from a first class ranges from 0% to 17% across 99 recorded first classes.
This is the cheapest conversion growth available: no new leads, no price change, only a decision about who stands in front of a newcomer.
Stop separating trainer assessment from the ledger
Studio Manager
The payroll scorecard rates trainers on conversion and retention over a cycle; this chapter measures what they actually delivered, class by class. The two currently do not inform each other.
One page a month that shows both, side by side, turns an opinion about a trainer into an argument with evidence.
Review the slots nobody attended, with the trainer in the room
Programming
11 classes ran to nobody, and 4 trainers carry at least one of them.
An empty class is usually an hour rather than a person; the review should decide which one it found before anyone is reassigned.

chapters.title: Memberships Lapsed and Churned
facts: 325 memberships were purchased in September, including 121 paid purchases with ₹13,96,809 recorded. The median observed follow-up was 8 days through month-end, not a completed lifetime. Thirty-day and longer checkpoints are unavailable for this purchase cohort.
Statuses and usage are export-state fields. Observed days through September 30 are not completed membership lifetime; checkpoints without mature purchases are unavailable.
chapters.subtitle: Recent purchases need time before retention can be judged
recs_extra: Write the unspent classes back as visits, with a date on them
Front Desk + Finance
11 memberships used a quarter or less of what they bought, leaving 127 classes undelivered worth about ₹12,53,970.
Converting credit into booked attendance moves money the studio already holds onto the balance sheet and pulls the member back into a routine - the single cheapest retention action available.
Segment win-back by recency, not by lifetime value
CRM + Marketing
81 people were here in the last thirty days and still hold ₹10,33,461; the largest group, 15 people, has not been inside a year.
Contact cost per recovered member falls by an order of magnitude between those two groups, and the studio currently sends the same message to both.
Freeze, do not lose: treat a pause request as a save
Front Desk
10 memberships were frozen at some point and 100.0% are still live, against 76.5% of those that were never frozen.
A member who asks to pause is planning to return. Offering the pause before they offer the cancellation converts a churn event into a deferred one.
Put every member on a plan at the halfway point of their membership
Studio Manager
85% of measurable memberships attended less in their second half than their first, and 64% attended at least half as often. The change is visible before the status moves.
A mid-membership review - attendance so far, what is left, one specific class to book - is the only intervention in this chapter that can act before the lapse rather than after it.

recs_extra: Rebuild PowerCycle around what actually fills
Programming + Founder
PowerCycle holds 35% of the timetable and fills 35%. The best-filling format in the studio, Hosted Class, gets 1%.
Moving ten per cent of PowerCycle’s classes into the hours and rooms that already fill is worth roughly 5,929 attendances a month at current prices.
Scale Hosted Class on purpose, and measure it
Programming + Marketing
Hosted Class fills 86% on 2 classes - the best in the studio and among the smallest programmes.
A format at capacity cannot tell the studio anything about demand. Doubling its classes for a month is the only way to learn whether the fill was scarcity or quality.
Set the complimentary budget by format, not by goodwill
Studio Manager + Finance
Mat 57 Express runs 10% free of charge, against 0% at the other end, on a month-wide utilisation of 42.6%.
A stated budget with a stated purpose converts an unmanaged subsidy into a marketing line the studio can switch off when the purpose is met.
Market the second format to the devoted, not to everyone
Marketing + Front Desk
94 members made three or more visits to one format this month and 38% of members touched more than one format. Frequency concentrates in the members who already come.
One named class offered to a member in their fourth week of a single format is the highest-yield cross-sell the studio has, and it costs nothing but the message.
Try the empty day, once, before calling it unfillable
Programming
42 format-and-day combinations had no class at all this month. The studio has never tested them.
One four-week trial per gap, with the same trainer and hour as the successful version, turns an assumption into a fact at the cost of one slot.

kpis.label: Value at average
kpis.detail: opportunity cost, not a booked loss

facts: 199 late-cancelled seats were recorded against 1,604 bookings: a 12.4% release rate. 1 booked seat was neither attended nor late-cancelled. Released capacity is not automatically lost revenue.
Released seats valued at average session revenue are an illustrative opportunity value, not a booked loss.
chapters.subtitle: Released seats are capacity to recover
recs_extra: Send the reminder four hours out, not twenty-four
Front Desk + Systems
Late releases peak at 09:00 with 39 seats in September 2026. The decision to skip is made on the day, not the day before.
A reminder placed inside the decision window is the only nudge that can still change the outcome, and a waitlist text sent at the same moment converts the release into an attendance.
Talk to the members who cancel repeatedly, one at a time
Studio Manager
29 members cancelled three or more times this month and the ten most frequent produced 24% of all late releases.
A short call costs nothing, and for a member cancelling around a scheduling conflict it fixes the pattern in a way no rule about credits would.
Charge for the seat that cannot be resold, and refund the one that can
Founder + Finance
199 seats came back late at 12.4% of the book, and the release rate differs more by hour than by trainer.
A rule anchored to resale feasibility is fair enough that staff will enforce it, and it stops the studio taxing an 18:30 class to solve a 07:00 problem.
Cap the depth of the largest code and publish the ceiling
Marketing + Finance
NC-2026-SHQ is 42% of all discounting in September 2026 at a mean depth of 19%.
One code at one depth is auditable. Four codes at four depths is a negotiation at the desk, and the desk always loses the argument it has to have twice a week.
Use the cancellation signal as an early warning, not a penalty
CRM + Studio Manager
Members with more than half their bookings cancelled are live 100% of the time against 77% for those who never cancel, on the selected-month membership-purchase cohort.
Reading a rising cancellation rate as an at-risk flag costs nothing and starts the retention conversation weeks before the lapse date.

chapters.subtitle: Read sales, seats and regular visits together
recs_extra: Manage frequency, not headcount
Founder + Studio Manager
Visits per member fell to 3.56 from 4.84 while the base moved to 394 from 305. The studio is serving 503 fewer visits than the same base produced a year ago.
One extra visit a month for a tenth of the base is worth roughly ₹46,777 of delivered revenue and moves renewal rates before it moves cash.
Use the other 3 studios as the control group
Founder
This studio ranks 2 of 4 on utilisation in September 2026 (42.6% against a group median of 40.6%).
Any month where the studio moves with the group is a market month; any month where it moves alone is a decision. That distinction saves the studio from reacting to weather.
Publish these four numbers on one page, monthly
Studio Manager

Leads, trials, bookings against capacity and visits per member all move before the figures the studio currently watches. In September 2026 they read 189 new leads, 1,604 booked seats and 3.56 visits per member.
A leading indicator nobody publishes is a leading indicator nobody changes.

chapters.subtitle: Trials and follow-ups show where prospects progress
recs_extra: Make the trial the only acquisition target
Sales + Studio Manager
Leads who completed a trial convert at 11.7% and those who did not at 0.0%. On this file that is 86 leads sitting on the wrong side of a diary entry.
Every lead conversation ends with a time and a class, not a callback. At the studio’s current trial-to-win rate, a hundred more trials is worth roughly 11 more members a year.
Answer on the day, because the win is decided the same day 2% of the time
Sales
The median first response in this file came after 2 days, and 66% of leads waited more than a day, while 100% of all wins closed on the day of the enquiry.
The lead is not waiting politely; they are calling the next studio on their list. A same-day response target with no exceptions is worth more than any change to the offer.
Move acquisition effort toward Website Form and Yellow Messenger/Whatsapp Enquiry
Marketing + Founder
Website Form converts at 15.0% with a mean LTV of ₹2,631 on 20 leads; the largest source, Website, converts at 4.1% on 74.
Tripling the smaller, better source costs less than the studio currently spends to fill the larger one and delivers members who stay longer.
Publish conversion by associate, with book size beside it
Studio Manager
Conversion runs 2.0% to 15.9% across books of 42 to 51 leads.
Putting the two columns together on one page every month ends the argument about whose leads are worse and starts the one about what each person does with theirs.
Report leads weekly, on the stage they are stuck at
Founder + Sales
24 leads were contacted at most once, and the file shows follow-ups spanning a median of 6 days for decisions that usually take one.
A weekly thirty-minute review of the stuck stages is the only cadence that matches how quickly a lead goes cold.

chapters.title: Member Behaviour and Patterns
facts: 394 community members made 1,404 attended visits, averaging 3.56 each. The same 78 returning members made 252 fewer visits than last September (35.3%).
One visit is not confirmed churn. Spend is recorded check-in revenue; preference is observed attendance, not a stated intention.
chapters.subtitle: Repeat visits tell the fuller attendance story
recs_extra: Give the 205 once-only members a dated plan, not a reminder
Front Desk + Studio Manager
205 of the 394 members who attended in September 2026 came exactly once, 52% of the base. They are not a churn statistic; they are the next month’s frequency problem.

One booked class with a time attached, offered before the member leaves the building, converts a visit into a habit. On this month’s numbers a tenth of that group attending twice more is 41 extra attendances.
Build the at-risk list from the member’s own gap, not from the studio’s
CRM

The studio-wide median gap between visits is 1 day, but the distribution runs from one day later to a tail beyond two months. A fixed thirty-day rule flags half the base and misses the members who always came weekly and have just stopped.
A gap that stretches past a member’s own median is the earliest reliable warning the data contains, and it is computable from the ledger the studio already exports each day.
Sell the next purchase 5 days after the last
Front Desk + Finance
The median gap between purchases at this studio is 5 days and 100% of repeat purchases fall inside a month. Beyond that window the probability of a second purchase falls away.
A renewal conversation scheduled to the member’s own purchase rhythm rather than the expiry date is the difference between a renewal and a re-acquisition.
Program the middle of the day on purpose, not by residue
Programming
16 members take midday as their habit against 249 morning and 129 evening, and the midday group comes 1.06 times a month against 3.72 at the peak.
One format scheduled specifically for the middle of the day, with an off-peak price attached, converts idle mid-morning capacity rather than competing for the evening.
Count the third visit, not the second, as the return
Marketing + Founder

10% of recorded first-timers came back once after their trial but only 6% reached a third visit. A 2-for-1 pack member is a returning client on their third visit, and every retention measure built on the second one is flattering the studio.
Fixing the definition changes what the team optimises for, and costs nothing but a column in the report.
Protect the frequent tenth as a named group
Studio Manager
39 members produced 42% of all attendance in September 2026. A fifth of them changing habit moves the month more than any acquisition campaign on file.
A monthly watch-list, one message when someone in it stops coming, and no discount, is the cheapest revenue protection the studio has.
